title: A continuum law for dense particulate flow from creep to inertia in an arbitrary shape

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a transferable continuum description of densely packed particles that predicts how a material moves, creeps or stops across different container shapes and flow regimes. Instead of tracking every particle, it would connect independently measured particle and surface properties to equations for material behavior. Combined with conservation laws and appropriate initial and boundary conditions, those equations would predict spatial velocity and stress fields.

The intended scope extends from slow, nearly static granular creep through dense suspensions dominated by liquid viscosity to rapid dense flows dominated by particle inertia. It also encompasses particle shape, size distributions, friction and adhesion. Nonlocality is central: motion at one location can depend on rearrangements elsewhere, so the material response cannot always be determined from local stress and shear rate alone. The goal is to integrate and extend existing predictive models across these conditions, rather than to introduce the first continuum description of granular flow.

significance.text: Dense particulate materials occur in industrial processing and geophysical flows. A framework that transfers between geometries and materials would make it possible to predict where motion concentrates, how far creeping regions extend and when a change in confinement causes flow to stop. These are direct consequences of a successful constitutive description within its validated range. Existing models already provide some of these predictions; the revolutionary advance would be achieving substantially broader transferability with independently determined material parameters.

Conditional impact assessment: such a capability could reduce repeated geometry-specific calibration and support the design of handling equipment, processing conditions and particulate formulations. Connecting a controlled surface-friction change to a predicted thickening boundary would be especially valuable because it would link particle engineering to bulk flow behavior. These downstream uses would still require reliable surface measurements, suitable boundary descriptions and validation for the intended operating conditions.

The comparison with continuum field equations for simple fluids expresses the ambition of the innovation, not an established historical equivalence. A constitutive law alone does not determine a flow: conservation equations, geometry, loading history, initial conditions and boundary conditions also matter. Even a successful demonstration in several containers would establish a bounded predictive capability, not literal applicability to every container or automatic formulation of an industrial slurry.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a reliably transferable description across the combined material and flow scope. Local inertial-number rheology can fail in spatially inhomogeneous flows, particularly where grain-scale nonlocality controls creep or geometry-dependent arrest. Spatial variation in shear rate does not by itself make every local prediction fail. Nor is mathematical well-posedness wholly missing: some existing nonlocal granular models already possess it. The harder integration problem is to retain predictive and mathematical reliability while spanning creep, viscous suspensions, inertia and realistic particle properties.

Concrete barriers include determining the physical meaning and parameters of nonlocal constitutive equations, selecting justified boundary conditions and representing the intrinsic length scales that govern confinement and arrest. For example, predicting a critical nozzle opening for jamming requires a length scale related to the particulate structure. A model that fits homogeneous rheometry must therefore acquire additional spatial information without relying on a new fit for every geometry.

Realistic suspensions add strong polydispersity, nonspherical particles, surface interactions, boundaries and transient histories. The 2026 perspective describes limited treatment of strongly unequal particle sizes and nonspherical geometries in many simulation frameworks, alongside challenges in microstructural calibration and continuum closure. Resolving particle-scale interactions while predicting macroscopic flow makes the problem inherently multiscale and computationally demanding.

Frictional-contact frameworks explain important features of discontinuous shear thickening and shear jamming, but this explanatory success does not establish a universal design rule for realistic particle mixtures. The reviewed perspective relates their volume-fraction boundaries to friction coefficients while also discussing semi-quantitative agreement and fitted friction values exceeding measured values. Predicting bulk behavior from independently measured contact properties remains a substantive challenge. Adhesion and agglomeration belong to the intended scope, although the separate British Society of Rheology review cited for their reconciliation difficulties could not be checked from the supplied source material.

current_state.text: Kamrin’s 2019 review documents quantitative nonlocal predictions of creep in multiple two-dimensional experiments, selected three-dimensional flows including split-bottom cells, and geometry-dependent stopping thresholds. It also reports Hadamard well-posedness for nonlocal granular fluidity, or NGF, and certain strongly nonlocal models. Thus inhomogeneous flow, creep and cessation are already predictive achievements in selected settings. The open goal is their integration and transfer across a much wider range of materials and regimes.

That review also identifies unresolved interpretation of phenomenological equations and uncertainty in boundary-condition selection. Its annular Couette discussion illustrates the motivation for nonlocal descriptions: slow creep occurs throughout a geometry where a local yield-based treatment would predict an immobile region. The supplied evidence review relied on retained article narrative that omitted several displayed equations; figures were not inspected. These limitations constrain independent assessment of the detailed mathematics and visual comparisons without negating the reported narrative findings.

“Recent Modeling Advances in Dense Suspension Rheology” was submitted to arXiv on 12 March 2026 and revised on 5 June 2026. The supplied review assessed a complete 17-page text extraction and verified its account of multiscale computational difficulty, continuum and particle-based advances, and remaining challenges involving realistic particle properties, boundaries, transient histories and calibration. It is a perspective preprint; journal publication was not confirmed. Its discussion supports an unfinished integration problem, but does not prove that no model anywhere meets the full proposed scope.

The research identifies a 2024 Annual Review article, “Advances in Modeling Dense Granular Media,” attributed to Kamrin, Hill, Goldman and Andrade, as surveying roughly fifteen years of progress from local inertial-number rheology toward nonlocality, polydispersity and particle shape. It also identifies a September 2024 invited paper, “Rheology of dense granular suspensions across flow regimes,” as proposing viscous-to-inertial superposition for hard-sphere suspensions. Neither article had saved text available to the supplied evidence review. Their reported contents remain relevant leads, but their precise scope and the claimed unification cannot be independently established here.

The research also reports a 2026 PNAS emulsion experiment, with an acceptance date of 21 July 2026, in which accounting for a pressure-dependent shift in jamming reportedly brings emulsion flow into agreement with granular-suspension rules. No saved article text was supplied for review, so the result, date, experimental scope and degree of agreement remain unverified here. In particular, accounting for a jamming shift should not be described as removing jamming itself. Even if confirmed, agreement in the studied flow conditions would not by itself establish the proposed law across nonlocal creep, arbitrary geometries and realistic surfaces.

The British Society of Rheology review is reported in the research as published on 30 September 2026 and as identifying unresolved reconciliation for variable friction and adhesion-driven agglomeration. Only an indexed passage and bibliographic information were supplied, without saved article text, so that attribution remains unverified. These access limitations are not evidence that the cited findings are false. Separately, the supplied material contains no bounded search record establishing completeness through 1 November 2026; the dated findings therefore cannot establish the absence of a later or overlooked solution.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: fix one model’s material parameters using only homogeneous rheometry or independently measured particle properties, then predict three withheld experiments on the same material: an inhomogeneous creeping flow, a rapid dense flow and a geometry-dependent stopping threshold. Include at least one rough, polydisperse suspension rather than relying entirely on monodisperse dry spheres. This three-experiment requirement is a proposed benchmark, not an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: One independently calibrated model predicts three withheld flow experiments

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: specify initial conditions, loading histories, independently justified boundary conditions, measurement protocols and quantitative acceptance tolerances before the withheld tests. Compare predicted velocity fields and stopping thresholds with measurements and their uncertainties. Publish enough material characterization, equations, parameter values and computational details for independent reproduction, and test whether results remain predictive without geometry-specific refitting.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce withheld predictions under prespecified protocols without geometry-specific refitting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed formulation test: predict the thickening boundary following a controlled change in surface friction before the new batch is mixed. Independently characterize the changed surface properties so that agreement cannot be obtained by selecting a friction coefficient after observing the bulk response. This proposal addresses the reviewed gap between friction-based explanations and independently calibrated prediction; the exact pre-mixing requirement is an additional proposed criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Predict thickening boundaries before mixing from measured surface properties

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope assessment: examine mathematical well-posedness separately from agreement with experiments, and extend validation across additional geometries, particle shapes, size distributions, adhesion strengths and transient histories before claiming that breadth. State the demonstrated ranges and practical computational requirements. Finite experiments can establish transferability over tested conditions; they cannot prove universality for arbitrary shapes, materials or containers.
completion_criteria.label: Assess well-posedness separately and report validated scope and computational requirements

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: RHE-01, a constitutive closure that works in a flow it was not fitted to, shares the central demand for transferability. RHE-03 makes that demand specific to dense particulate materials, nonlocality, confinement and the creep-to-inertia range. RHE-02, predictive amorphous yielding, overlaps in arrest and the onset of motion, but its stated target is yield stress and brittle versus ductile failure rather than the full particulate flow field.

Roster-based comparison: RHE-07, measurement of local three-dimensional stress without assuming a constitutive law, could provide independent evidence for testing RHE-03. Its objective is measurement rather than closure. RHE-10, a constitutive law for magma containing crystals and bubbles, overlaps through dense multiphase flow, but explicitly includes bubbles and magma-specific material behavior that a dense-particle law would not automatically cover.

Roster-based comparison: RHE-04, inverse molecular design of polymer-melt rheology, and RHE-11, topology-based ring-polymer rheology, connect microscopic structure to macroscopic response through molecular mechanisms distinct from particulate contacts and confinement. RHE-08 targets elasto-inertial turbulence and drag reduction, while RHE-09 targets computation of highly elastic viscoelastic flows. Their constitutive and computational challenges are related in broad purpose, but achieving RHE-03 would not establish those capabilities.

Roster-based comparison: RHE-05 seeks invertible active-stress control for a mechanical task, and RHE-06 seeks addressable solid–fluid switching that persists without a sustaining field or settling particles. They concern designed actuation and switching rather than the predictive description of creep, flow and arrest targeted here. Friction-controlled thickening may provide a point of contact, but passive flow prediction does not itself supply persistent switching or active control.

Within RHE-03, nonlocal confined flow and the inclusion of shape, friction and polydispersity are complementary parts of the same integration goal. The research’s assertion that historical items 5 and 9 duplicate this concept cannot be checked because those historical entries were not supplied. Their numbering must not be equated with the present roster’s RHE-05 and RHE-09, which describe distinct innovations.

change_log.change: Qualified the claim that local inertial-number rheology fails whenever shear rate varies spatially.
change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence supports failures in relevant nonlocal regimes, not automatic failure in every inhomogeneous flow.

change_log.change: Integrated existing quantitative creep, three-dimensional flow and stopping-threshold predictions, together with well-posedness results for selected nonlocal models.
change_log.reason: These achievements correct the earlier implication that such capabilities remain wholly undemonstrated.

change_log.change: Defined the missing breakthrough as broad integration and transferability with independently determined parameters.
change_log.reason: This preserves the concept while avoiding an unsupported claim that no well-posed or predictive continuum models exist.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 2024 and 2026 advances with explicit limits on verification and scope.
change_log.reason: Missing source text prevents confirmation but does not justify deleting the claims or treating them as false.

change_log.change: Rephrased the reported emulsion result as accounting for a pressure-dependent jamming shift.
change_log.reason: The supplied description does not support saying that jamming itself was removed.

change_log.change: Separated verified preprint dates and findings from unconfirmed journal publication and completeness through November 2026.
change_log.reason: The perspective was reviewed, but publication and freshness were not established.

change_log.change: Preserved boundary-condition, microstructural calibration, friction-parameter and extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: These scientific and access distinctions materially affect interpretation of existing capabilities.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration with advance tolerances, reproducibility, independent calibration and separate mathematical assessment.
change_log.reason: Three successful experiments would establish bounded transferability rather than arbitrary-geometry universality.

change_log.change: Qualified the simple-fluid analogy and downstream formulation benefits.
change_log.reason: Prediction also requires conservation equations, initial and boundary conditions, material inputs and application-specific validation.

change_log.change: Replaced the unverified detailed application inventory with the supported industrial and geophysical motivation, and compared the supplied roster without merging entries.
change_log.reason: The review did not establish every listed application or the asserted overlap with absent historical items.

unresolved_issues: Whether any existing model already achieves the full combined scope remains unresolved; the supplied material does not establish universal nonexistence.
The Annual Review article, 2024 viscous-to-inertial paper, 2026 emulsion experiment and British Society of Rheology review lack saved text for confirming their reported details.
The emulsion experiment’s exact pressure correction, material conditions and breadth of agreement remain unverified.
Journal publication of the 2026 perspective and completeness of the literature assessment through 1 November 2026 remain unestablished.
The supplied review’s 2019 narrative extraction omitted several displayed equations and did not include figure inspection, limiting assessment of detailed mathematical and visual evidence.
Quantitative benchmark tolerances, material-property ranges and acceptable computational requirements still need to be specified.
Historical items 5 and 9 were not supplied, so their asserted overlap cannot be resolved.

brief.title: Predicting when packed particles flow or stop
possible: Engineers could predict where packed grains or particles in liquid will move, creep slowly or stop as a container changes shape. The same equations would cover slow motion and rapid flow, using measured particle properties instead of tracking every particle.

They could also predict how changing particle surfaces affects thickening, when a mixture becomes harder to stir or pump. That would connect choices about particles to the behavior of the whole mixture.
why: People designing handling equipment and industrial mixtures could spend less effort tuning a model for each container. Predictions of where flow concentrates and where material stops would help them choose equipment shapes and processing conditions.
For researchers studying flows of earth materials, the benefit would be a shared description across conditions now handled by different models.

sources.showed: This review discusses unresolved modeling problems involving changing friction and adhesion, the sticking that can make particles clump.
sources.cited_for: It supports including friction and particle sticking among the challenges.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a predictive law spanning these interactions and the full range of flows.

sources.showed: This review surveys progress in modeling packed grains, including effects of distant rearrangements, unequal particle sizes and particle shape.
sources.cited_for: It supports the case that existing models already address parts of the proposed scope.
sources.not_established: It does not establish that these capabilities work together in one transferable model.

sources.showed: The review describes models that predict slow creep and stopping in selected settings. It explains nonlocality: motion depends on particle rearrangements elsewhere.
sources.quote: However, slow, creeping flow is seen throughout the entire geometry.
sources.cited_for: It supports the need to account for distant motion and particle size when predicting creep and stopping.
sources.not_established: Success in selected flows does not establish transfer across liquids, rapid flows and realistic particle mixtures.

sources.who: Authors of the suspension flow study
sources.showed: This paper proposes combining contributions from liquid resistance and particle inertia, the tendency of moving particles to keep moving, for suspensions of hard spheres.
sources.cited_for: It supports connecting flows governed by liquid resistance with those governed by particle inertia.
sources.not_established: It does not establish predictions spanning slow creep, varied container shapes and realistic particle surfaces.

sources.showed: This experiment studies whether accounting for a pressure-dependent change in jamming, when particles become stuck, brings emulsions into agreement with rules for grain suspensions.
sources.cited_for: It supports investigating shared flow rules across different kinds of packed materials.
sources.not_established: Agreement under the studied conditions would not establish broad predictions of creep, stopping and surface effects.

sources.who: Orhun Ayar, Bhargav Sriram Siddani, Ishan Srivastava and Abhinendra Singh
sources.showed: This perspective preprint reviews simulations linking particle contacts and liquid forces to mixture flow. Its main focus is conditions dominated by liquid resistance.
sources.cited_for: It supports the importance of particle interactions and the difficulty of connecting particle behavior to whole flows.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate one independently calibrated model across the proposed materials and flow conditions.

shown: Kamrin’s review describes quantitative predictions of slow creep, selected flows through a volume, and stopping that depends on confinement. Some models also have established mathematical reliability. Predicting creep and stopping is already possible in selected settings.
missing: A shared model still needs to demonstrate transfer from slow creep to liquid-dominated and rapid flows without fresh fitting for each container.
Predictions need justified descriptions of wall interactions and the particle-scale distances that govern creep and stopping.
Measured surface properties still need to predict thickening reliably for mixtures with varied particle sizes, shapes and sticking.

milestones.label: One model predicts three withheld flow experiments
milestones.explanation: One independently calibrated model would have to predict withheld creep, rapid flow and confinement-dependent stopping, including a rough suspension with varied particle sizes. This would test transfer across flow conditions.

milestones.label: Independent tests reproduce predictions without fitting each container
milestones.explanation: Independent tests would have to reproduce motion and stopping predictions under preset conditions, histories, wall rules and tolerances, with enough detail to repeat them. This would test whether prediction survives without fresh fitting.

milestones.label: Measured surfaces predict thickening before mixing
milestones.explanation: Measured changes in surface friction would have to predict when thickening begins before a new batch is mixed. This would connect particle design to mixture behavior without choosing friction values afterward.

milestones.label: Mathematical reliability and tested scope are established
milestones.explanation: Mathematical reliability would need separate assessment, alongside tests across shapes, sizes, sticking and flow histories, with computing needs stated. This would establish where the law works and how practical it is.

uncertain: Whether an existing model already covers the full combined range remains unresolved.
The required accuracy, material ranges and acceptable computing demands for judging success remain open.
